Shabbetai Tzvi.event: Shabbetai Tzvi is born in Smyrna, conventionally on 9 Av 5386 (1 August 1626), to Mordecai Tzvi, an agent for European merchants, and his wife. The symbolically charged 9 Av date may have been retrospectively aligned with the tradition that the Messiah would be born on the anniversary of the Temple’s destruction. Tzvi receives a Talmudic education, studies Kabbalah and is prepared for the local scholarly elite. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica account and National Library of Israel.

Around 1648, Shabbetai Tzvi begins openly presenting himself as the Messiah and performs acts—including pronouncing the divine name—that alarm Smyrna’s communal authorities. Opposition and bans eventually force him from the city; sources do not support a single precise expulsion date. See YIVO Encyclopedia and the Treccani historical dictionary.

After leaving Smyrna in the early 1650s, Shabbetai Tzvi seeks a receptive audience in the major Kabbalistic center of Salonica. A theatrical marriage ceremony between himself and a Torah scroll intensifies opposition, and local authorities compel him to leave. The year is approximate within a poorly dated period of wandering. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and YIVO Encyclopedia.

By 1658, Shabbetai Tzvi is in Constantinople, one of several stops during his post-Smyrna wandering. He meets the preacher and Kabbalist Abraham Yachini, later an important propagandist, and continues public symbolic rituals that mix asceticism, messianic self-presentation and violations of established practice. See the Encyclopaedia Judaica account.

Around 1660, Shabbetai Tzvi settles in Cairo for approximately two years and gains the support of Raphael Joseph Chelebi, the wealthy Jewish mint-master and communal patron. This relationship later connects Tzvi with Jerusalem’s fundraising needs and helps finance the emerging movement. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and CET Hebrew biography.

Shabbetai Tzvi moves to Jerusalem and lives ascetically among its Jewish community. Despite concern over his behaviour, community leaders entrust him with a fundraising mission to Cairo. The surviving narratives differ over the exact duration and sequence, so this entry avoids claiming an exact arrival day. See CET historical lexicon and the Encyclopaedia Judaica account.

While serving Jerusalem’s fundraising mission in Cairo, Shabbetai Tzvi receives renewed backing from Raphael Joseph Chelebi and marries Sarah, a Jewish refugee whose own earlier history became heavily polemicized by supporters and opponents. The marriage is interpreted within his developing messianic symbolism. See CET Hebrew biography and the Jewish Encyclopedia.

In April 1665, Shabbetai Tzvi travels to Gaza seeking a spiritual remedy from Nathan of Gaza. Instead, Nathan identifies him as the Messiah and supplies the Kabbalistic interpretation and energetic correspondence that turn a personal claim into a mass movement. On 31 May Tzvi publicly proclaims his messianic role in Gaza. See the detailed Encyclopaedia Judaica chronology and CET Hebrew account.

After renewed conflict in Jerusalem, Shabbetai Tzvi travels north toward Smyrna and receives an enthusiastic reception in Aleppo. His physical journey and Nathan of Gaza’s letters together carry the movement into the great Jewish commercial networks of the eastern Mediterranean. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and YIVO Encyclopedia.

Returning to Smyrna in autumn 1665, Shabbetai Tzvi becomes the focus of mass acclaim and severe communal coercion. In December he publicly proclaims himself the anointed redeemer, changes synagogue practice, appoints followers to imagined kingdoms and announces redemption for 1666. Contemporary evidence also records substantial opposition; enthusiasm was never literally unanimous. See the scholarly chronology and the Turkish TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi.

Shabbetai Tzvi.place: Abydos fortress near Gallipoli, Ottoman Empire
Shabbetai Tzvi.event: Sailing toward Constantinople in February 1666, Shabbetai Tzvi is arrested by Ottoman authorities and eventually confined in the fortress of Abydos near Gallipoli. Followers rename the prison Migdal Oz, visit in large numbers and supply enough money for an unusually comfortable confinement, while movement-wide expectation reaches its height. See the Jewish Encyclopedia and Center for Online Judaic Studies.

Taken to the imperial court at Adrianople, Shabbetai Tzvi converts to Islam on 16 September 1666 after Ottoman proceedings over the political danger attributed to his movement. He adopts the name Aziz Mehmed Efendi, receives an honorary court position and stipend, and outwardly enters Muslim life. Accounts that reduce the episode to a simple theatrical choice between immediate torture and conversion are later narrative formulations; Ottoman evidence is sparse. See the scholarly reassessment of the conversion and the Turkish TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi.

After years of publicly Muslim but religiously ambiguous activity and continuing contact with Jewish followers, Shabbetai Tzvi again attracts Ottoman suspicion. In January 1673 he is exiled to the Adriatic fortress-town of Dulcigno, where he receives visitors and continues correspondence under confinement. See the Ulcinj tourism authority’s local history and Encyclopaedia Judaica.

Shabbetai Tzvi dies in exile, traditionally on Yom Kippur, 10 Tishrei 5437 (commonly converted as 17 September 1676), aged fifty. Competing burial traditions later placed his grave at Ulcinj or Berat; twentieth-century research and local tradition favour Ulcinj, but the precise grave identification remains disputed. See the Ulcinj local historical account, Pe’amim study of the grave tradition and National Library of Israel discussion.

Edmond James de Rothschild.event: Edmond James de Rothschild is born at Boulogne-Billancourt on 19 August 1845, the youngest son of James Mayer de Rothschild and Betty von Rothschild, leaders of the Paris branch of the banking family. His Hebrew name is Benjamin. See the Rothschild Archive family biography and National Library of Israel.

At twenty-three, Edmond James de Rothschild joins the family’s Paris banking house. He also becomes involved in the Chemin de fer de l’Est and develops the collecting, scientific and philanthropic interests that distinguish his career from banking alone. See the Rothschild Archive.

During the Franco-Prussian War, Edmond James de Rothschild serves in the French Garde Mobile. His service takes place amid the siege, regime change and communal crisis of 1870–1871 rather than as a permanent military career. See the Rothschild Archive family biography.

In late 1882, Edmond James de Rothschild separately meets Samuel Mohilever and Yechiel Brill, who propose a colony for experienced Jewish farmers, and Joseph Feinberg, who seeks emergency help for Rishon LeZion. Against the background of Russian pogroms and mass migration, these approaches begin his sustained Palestine settlement programme. See the Ramat Hanadiv timeline and its detailed Hebrew history.

Edmond James de Rothschild.place: Rishon LeZion and the First Aliyah colonies, Ottoman Palestine
Edmond James de Rothschild.event: On his first Palestine visit, Edmond James de Rothschild and his wife Adelheid arrive anonymously through Jaffa in April 1887 and inspect Rishon LeZion, Zikhron Ya’akov and other colonies supported through his administrators. The journey lets him assess five years of agricultural investment directly. See the Ramat Hanadiv chronology and Rothschild Archive.

Edmond James de Rothschild makes his second Palestine visit, a brief inspection centred on Zikhron Ya’akov. The colony, renamed for his father James, had become a focus of vineyard and winery development as well as recurring conflict between farmers and the baron’s officials. See the Ramat Hanadiv’s Hebrew history.

During his third visit, Edmond James de Rothschild reviews both the colonies’ achievements and the costly, conflict-ridden system of direct administration. At the end of 1899 he transfers ownership of the settlements and fifteen million francs to the Jewish Colonization Association, which assumes administration in 1900 while he continues financial support. See the Rothschild Archive and Ramat Hanadiv.

Edmond James de Rothschild.place: Umm el-Aleq, southern Carmel, Ottoman Palestine
Edmond James de Rothschild.event: On his fourth Palestine visit in February 1914, Edmond James de Rothschild tours the southern Carmel ridge near Zikhron Ya’akov and expresses the wish to be buried there ‘in the rock.’ His will later specifies burial in Palestine. The site becomes Ramat Hanadiv after his death. See Ramat Hanadiv’s garden history.

Edmond James de Rothschild reorganizes the Palestine section of the Jewish Colonization Association as the Palestine Jewish Colonization Association (PICA), placing his son James at its head. Incorporated in Palestine on 15 April 1924, PICA administers land and directs new agricultural and industrial investment while maintaining a Paris office. See the original memorandum and articles and Rothschild Archive.

Edmond James de Rothschild.place: Tel Aviv and the Jewish settlements, Mandatory Palestine
Edmond James de Rothschild.event: At eighty, Edmond James de Rothschild makes his fifth and final tour of Palestine. Welcomed publicly across a much enlarged Yishuv, he addresses the Great Synagogue in Tel Aviv and presents the journey as evidence that the settlement programme begun in 1882 had become durable. See Ramat Hanadiv’s five-visit history and Yad Hanadiv timeline.

Edmond James de Rothschild.place: Boulogne-Billancourt and Père Lachaise Cemetery, Paris, France
Edmond James de Rothschild.event: Edmond James de Rothschild dies on 2 November 1934, aged eighty-nine. He is temporarily buried at Père Lachaise, pending fulfilment of his wish for burial in the land where he had supported Jewish settlement. The occasional date 30 November is contradicted by the principal institutional chronology. See the Ramat Hanadiv timeline, Rothschild Archive and Knesset biography.

On 6 April 1954, the remains of Edmond James de Rothschild and his wife Adelheid are brought from France aboard an Israeli naval vessel and reinterred in a state ceremony in the memorial crypt at Ramat Hanadiv. The posthumous movement fulfils the burial instruction in his will. See Ramat Hanadiv crypt history and the institutional timeline.

Israel Zangwill.event: Israel Zangwill is born in London on 21 January 1864, the eldest child of Moses Zangwill and Ellen Hannah Marks, impoverished Jewish immigrants from the Russian Empire. Some older references give 14 February, but modern authority records and scholarship use 21 January. See the Posen Library, National Library of Israel and Oxford Reference authority entry.

During his early childhood, Israel Zangwill lives with his family in Plymouth and then Bristol, where he receives his first schooling. The surviving summaries do not provide a precise year-by-year itinerary, so 1867 is an approximate marker for this childhood phase. See Oxford Bibliographies and the contemporary 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica biography.

The family returns to London when Zangwill is about eight. He enters the Jews’ Free School in Spitalfields, becomes a pupil-teacher and later teaches its senior class, gaining intimate knowledge of East End Jewish life that shapes his fiction. See the Jewish Museum London and Oxford Bibliographies.

While working as a teacher, Israel Zangwill completes a University of London degree with honours in English, French, and mental and moral science. He soon leaves teaching for journalism, editing and literary work. See the Jewish Virtual Library biography and Poetry Foundation.

Zangwill publishes Children of the Ghetto, commissioned by the Jewish Publication Society of America and issued in London by William Heinemann. Its portrayal of East End Jewish society establishes his international literary reputation. See the University of Delaware Special Collections, Posen Library and a scholarly reassessment in the Journal of Victorian Culture.

Israel Zangwill meets Theodor Herzl during Herzl’s first London visit. In 1896 he helps arrange Herzl’s address to the Maccabaeans, an important early platform for political Zionism in Britain. See the Posen Library and Encyclopedia Judaica biography.

Zangwill joins the Maccabaean pilgrimage to Palestine, travelling through Jerusalem and several Jewish settlements. The journey gives him direct experience of the country before he attends the First Zionist Congress later that year. See the University of Southampton Parkes Institute and the Encyclopaedia Judaica account of the Maccabaeans.

Israel Zangwill attends the First Zionist Congress as a visitor and becomes a prominent English-language advocate and speaker for the movement, although his commitment centres increasingly on Jewish political autonomy and immediate refuge. See the ANU Museum of the Jewish People and Encyclopedia Judaica.

Zangwill marries novelist and women’s-rights activist Edith Ayrton. Their intellectual and political partnership later includes public support for militant and constitutional suffrage organizations. See Oxford Bibliographies and the Mapping Women’s Suffrage research project.

When the Seventh Zionist Congress rejects further consideration of the British East Africa proposal, Israel Zangwill leads the territorialist break with the Zionist Organization. The proposal concerned land in present-day Kenya, despite its conventional ‘Uganda’ label. See the Posen Library and Oxford Bibliographies in Jewish Studies.

Zangwill becomes the central founder and president of the Jewish Territorial Organization, which seeks an autonomous Jewish refuge wherever a viable territory can be secured. Its commissions investigate possibilities in Africa, Australia, Canada, Mexico and elsewhere, but obtain no homeland. See the contemporary Jewish Encyclopedia, the Posen Library and the University of Southampton Zangwill papers guide.

Israel and Edith Zangwill acquire Far End in East Preston from artist Henry Holiday. Zangwill extends the house and uses it as his principal later-life home while continuing literary and political work in Britain and abroad. See the East Preston Parish Council heritage survey.

Zangwill’s play The Melting Pot opens at Washington’s Columbia Theatre on 5 October 1908 before an audience including President Theodore Roosevelt. Its immigrant drama widely popularizes the ‘melting pot’ metaphor. Surviving correspondence shows Roosevelt’s engagement with the play and permission for its dedication. See the Theodore Roosevelt Digital Library and Library of Congress correspondence and the Posen Library.

Zangwill and Edith Ayrton join the organized boycott of the 1911 census to protest women’s political exclusion. He speaks for multiple suffrage groups, supports the Jewish League for Woman Suffrage in 1912 and becomes a vice-president of the United Suffragists in 1914. See the Mapping Women’s Suffrage biographical record and a scholarly study in Women’s History Review.

Following the Balfour Declaration, Israel Zangwill temporarily renews cooperation with mainstream Zionism while insisting that Jewish settlement requires meaningful autonomy rather than refuge alone. He later returns to territorialist criticism as the political and demographic obstacles in Palestine become clearer. See the Posen Library and Victorian Web scholarly biography.

Israel Zangwill dies in Midhurst on 1 August 1926, near his home at East Preston. His death closes a career that joined literary representation of Anglo-Jewry with Zionist, territorialist, suffrage and peace campaigns. See the Jewish Virtual Library, National Library of Israel and Posen Library.

Israel Zangwill.place: Golders Green and Willesden, London, England
Israel Zangwill.event: A Liberal Jewish funeral service is held for Zangwill at Golders Green Crematorium on 5 August 1926, after which his ashes are interred in the Liberal Jewish Cemetery at Willesden. See the contemporary Jewish Telegraphic Agency report and the London Museum history of Golders Green Crematorium.

Janusz Korczak.event: Henryk Goldszmit, later known as Janusz Korczak, is born on 22 July in Warsaw to Józef Goldszmit and Cecylia Gębicka, an assimilated Jewish family. The surviving evidence does not resolve whether the year was 1878 or 1879. See Korczakianum, Museum of Warsaw and the Polish Janusz Korczak Association biography.

Janusz Korczak.place: Imperial University of Warsaw, Warsaw, Russian Empire
Janusz Korczak.event: Goldszmit begins medical studies while teaching, writing and participating in Warsaw’s reform-minded intellectual life. He adopts the literary pseudonym Janusz Korczak, derived from a name in a historical novel and fixed in its altered form after a printing error. See the Korczakianum biography and Treblinka Museum literary overview.

Janusz Korczak.place: Manchuria, Russian Empire’s Russo-Japanese War zone
Janusz Korczak.event: After qualifying in medicine, Korczak is mobilized as a military doctor during the Russo-Japanese War and travels as far as Manchuria. The experience places paediatric and social work within the violence and mass deprivation of war. See the Korczakianum Polish institutional biography.

Janusz Korczak.place: Bersohn and Bauman Children’s Hospital, Warsaw, Russian Empire
Janusz Korczak.event: Korczak begins work at the Jewish community’s Bersohn and Bauman Children’s Hospital, serving there until 1912 and developing specialist paediatric experience alongside free care for poor families. See Korczakianum and POLIN Museum.

Korczak undertakes postgraduate medical study in Berlin, part of wider educational travel that also takes him to Switzerland, Paris and London. He studies paediatrics and European institutions for children rather than separating medicine from pedagogy. See the Korczakianum institutional biography.

Janusz Korczak.place: Dom Sierot, 92 Krochmalna Street, Warsaw, Russian Empire
Janusz Korczak.event: Korczak becomes director of the purpose-built Dom Sierot for Jewish children, working with principal administrator Stefania Wilczyńska. The home develops a children’s parliament, peer court, noticeboard and newspaper as instruments of accountable communal life. See Korczakianum and the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia.

Janusz Korczak.place: Eastern Front and Kyiv region, Russian Empire
Janusz Korczak.event: Mobilized during the First World War, Korczak serves as a military physician on the Eastern Front and later works with children affected by war in Kyiv. His wartime observations feed the educational cycle later published as How to Love a Child. See the Korczakianum biography.

Janusz Korczak.place: Nasz Dom, Pruszków, Second Polish Republic
Janusz Korczak.event: Korczak and educator Maria Falska establish the pedagogical programme of Nasz Dom for Polish working-class and war-orphaned children. The institution extends his self-government methods beyond Dom Sierot while retaining a distinct administration. See Korczakianum.

Korczak founds Mały Przegląd, a weekly supplement to the Polish Jewish newspaper Nasz Przegląd. Children serve as correspondents and help determine its subjects, creating an unusually sustained public forum for young people until 1939. See Korczakianum.

Janusz Korczak.place: Nasz Dom, Bielany, Warsaw, Second Polish Republic
Janusz Korczak.event: Nasz Dom moves from Pruszków to a new building in Warsaw’s Bielany district. Korczak continues advising and researching there while directing Dom Sierot, lecturing and serving as a court expert in cases concerning children. See the Korczakianum biography.

Korczak visits Mandatory Palestine and lives for several weeks at kibbutz Ein Harod, studying collective education and renewing relationships with former pupils. The journey deepens his Jewish national interest without erasing his Polish cultural attachment. See Korczakianum and the Polish Janusz Korczak Association photographic archive.

Janusz Korczak.place: Ein Harod and Jerusalem, Mandatory Palestine
Janusz Korczak.event: Korczak returns to Palestine, again examining kibbutz childhood and the relationship between Polish and Jewish futures. He considers possibilities there but ultimately returns to Warsaw, where his institutions and responsibilities remain. See the Korczakianum biography and Korczak Association archive.

Germany invades Poland. Korczak supports the orphanage through siege and occupation, sometimes wearing his Polish officer’s uniform and refusing to accept occupation rules that humiliate Jews. His radio and children’s-press work ends as institutions are destroyed or censored. See the Korczakianum biography and USHMM.

Janusz Korczak.place: Dom Sierot, 33 Chłodna Street, Warsaw Ghetto
Janusz Korczak.event: German authorities force Dom Sierot from Krochmalna Street into the sealed Warsaw Ghetto. Korczak and Wilczyńska move with the children to crowded premises at 33 Chłodna and struggle for food, medicine and institutional continuity. See the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia and Korczakianum.

Janusz Korczak.place: Dom Sierot, 16 Sienna / 9 Śliska Street, Warsaw Ghetto
Janusz Korczak.event: The orphanage is displaced again to 16 Sienna, connected with 9 Śliska. Despite starvation and Korczak’s declining health, the staff preserve lessons, performances and children’s communal routines; he repeatedly seeks donations outside the home. See USHMM and the Maria Grzegorzewska University Warsaw site study.

From May until 4 August, Korczak writes the surviving Ghetto Diary. On 18 July the orphanage stages Rabindranath Tagore’s The Post Office; claims that this was simply a rehearsal for death should be treated as interpretation rather than documented intention. See the Museum of Warsaw account of the wartime writings and the Polish Korczak Association chronology.

On 5 or 6 August, German forces order Dom Sierot’s approximately two hundred children and staff to the deportation point. Eyewitness evidence establishes that Korczak and Stefania Wilczyńska remained with the children; dramatic stories about a formal last-minute pardon differ and are not securely documented. See POLIN Museum, USHMM and Korczakianum.

Janusz Korczak.place: Treblinka II extermination camp, German-occupied Poland
Janusz Korczak.event: Korczak, Wilczyńska, their colleagues and the children are transported to Treblinka and murdered in the gas chambers on 5 or 6 August 1942. No individual grave exists. Their deaths belong to the mass murder of Warsaw Jewry during Operation Reinhard, not merely to an uplifting legend of personal sacrifice. See POLIN Museum, USHMM and Korczakianum.

Albert Einstein.place: Ulm, Kingdom of Württemberg, German Empire
Albert Einstein.event: Albert Einstein is born on 14 March 1879 in Ulm to Hermann Einstein and Pauline Koch, members of a largely secular Jewish family. See the Nobel Foundation biography and the Einstein Papers Project.

Albert Einstein.place: Munich, Kingdom of Bavaria, German Empire
Albert Einstein.event: The Einstein family moves to Munich, where Hermann Einstein and his brother Jakob operate an electrical-engineering business. Albert grows up there and attends the Luitpold Gymnasium before leaving Germany in 1894. See the Nobel Foundation and the American Institute of Physics historical exhibit.

Albert Einstein.place: Pavia and Milan, Kingdom of Italy
Albert Einstein.event: After his family’s business fails and they relocate to northern Italy, Einstein leaves school in Munich and joins them, spending time principally in Pavia and Milan. His exact movements within the region are less precisely documented than the overall transition. See the American Institute of Physics and the Einstein Papers Project.

After failing the Zürich Polytechnic entrance examination while still underage, Einstein attends the liberal Aargau Cantonal School in Aarau, receives his secondary diploma in 1896 and lives with the Winteler family. See the Nobel Foundation biography and the AIP exhibit.

Einstein renounces his Württemberg citizenship and enters the Swiss Federal Polytechnic, now ETH Zürich, to train as a mathematics and physics teacher. He graduates in 1900 and becomes a Swiss citizen in 1901. See the Nobel Foundation biography and the Einstein Papers Project.

Einstein begins work as a technical expert at the Swiss Patent Office. In Bern he marries Mileva Marić in 1903, completes his University of Zürich doctorate and develops the ideas behind his extraordinary scientific papers. See the Nobel Foundation biography and the Einstein Papers, volume 2.

During his annus mirabilis, Einstein publishes papers on light quanta and the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity and mass–energy equivalence; he also receives his doctorate from the University of Zürich. See the primary documents in The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, volume 2 and the Nobel Prize facts page.
Einstein leaves the Patent Office for an associate professorship in theoretical physics at the University of Zürich, beginning his full-time academic career. See the Nobel Foundation biography.

Einstein becomes professor of theoretical physics at the German University in Prague. The appointment lasts until 1912, when he returns to Zürich as a professor at ETH. See the Nobel Foundation biography and the Einstein Papers Project.

Einstein moves to Berlin as a member of the Prussian Academy of Sciences. He becomes director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics in 1917 and remains based in Berlin until Nazi persecution ends his German career. See the Nobel Foundation biography and the Einstein Papers Project.

Einstein completes the field equations of general relativity in November 1915. Observations of the 1919 solar eclipse later support the predicted deflection of starlight and make him a global celebrity. See the primary documents in The Collected Papers, volume 6 and the AIP historical exhibit.

Einstein travels through the United States with Chaim Weizmann to raise support for the proposed Hebrew University of Jerusalem. That year’s Nobel Prize in Physics—announced in 1922—is awarded to him for services to theoretical physics, especially the photoelectric law. See the Albert Einstein Archives at the Hebrew University and the Nobel Prize facts page.

During his only visit to Palestine, Einstein gives a scientific lecture at the future Hebrew University site on Mount Scopus and publicly supports the university project. He later serves on its governing bodies and leaves it his literary estate. See the Albert Einstein Archives, Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

While Einstein is abroad, Hitler becomes German chancellor. Einstein renounces German citizenship, does not return to Nazi Germany and settles at the newly founded Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where he continues work on gravitation and unified-field theories. See the Institute for Advanced Study scholar record, the Einstein Papers Project and the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.

Albert Einstein.place: Peconic, Long Island, New York, United States
Albert Einstein.event: At physicist Leó Szilárd’s urging, Einstein signs a letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt warning that uranium could enable exceptionally powerful bombs and that Germany might pursue them. Einstein does not work on the Manhattan Project and later campaigns against nuclear arms. See the transcription and contextual record of the Einstein–Szilárd letter and the Einstein Papers Project.

Einstein becomes a United States citizen while retaining Swiss citizenship. From Princeton he increasingly speaks for refugees, civil rights, international government and nuclear disarmament. See the American Institute of Physics historical exhibit and the Einstein Papers Project.

After Chaim Weizmann’s death, the Israeli government offers Einstein the largely ceremonial presidency of Israel. He declines, explaining that he lacks the aptitude and experience for official duties involving people. See the Albert Einstein Archives, Hebrew University of Jerusalem and the Einstein Papers Project.

Einstein dies at Princeton Hospital on 18 April 1955 after an abdominal aortic aneurysm. He is cremated and has no conventional grave; his literary rights and papers pass to the Hebrew University of Jerusalem under his will. See the Nobel Foundation biography, the Institute for Advanced Study and the Albert Einstein Archives.

Sarah Schenirer.event: Sarah Schenirer is born in Kraków to Bezalel (Zalel) Schenirer and Roza Lack Schenirer. The civil register gives 3 July 1883 Julian, equivalent to 15 July Gregorian; this calendar difference explains conflicting modern dates. See the University of Toronto Bais Yaakov Project, Jewish Religious Community of Kraków and the YIVO Encyclopedia.

Around age fourteen, Schenirer leaves Polish school after completing the eighth grade because of family financial pressure and trains as a seamstress. Her father supplies religious books in Yiddish, enabling the self-education denied to her in formal Jewish institutions. The exact year is approximate. See the Bais Yaakov Project timeline and the Jewish Women’s Archive biography reproduced by My Jewish Learning.

Schenirer marries Shmuel Nussbaum. Her surviving Polish diary records an unhappy marriage and her eventual insistence on divorce in 1913, a chapter omitted from older movement biographies. See the University of Toronto scholarly timeline and the University of Wrocław Polish-Jewish autobiography project.

After the outbreak of the First World War, Schenirer joins Galician Jewish refugees in Vienna. At the Stumpergasse Synagogue she hears Moshe David Flesch preach a German neo-Orthodox interpretation of Jewish history and duty, an experience she later identifies as decisive for her educational mission. See the Bais Yaakov Project biography, YIVO Encyclopedia and the University of Wrocław.

After returning from Vienna, Schenirer organizes religious study for young women and an Orthodox Girls’ Union. She concludes that durable religious education must begin with school-age girls rather than rely only on adult lectures. See the University of Toronto Bais Yaakov Project and YIVO Encyclopedia.

Before opening her school, Schenirer seeks the blessing of Yissachar Dov Rokeach, the Belzer Rebbe, at Marienbad. Accounts differ over how fully she described her proposal and note that the Belz court did not initially send its own girls, so the encounter should not be read as universal Hasidic endorsement. See the Bais Yaakov Project and the sourced overview and competing testimony summarized on Wikipedia.

In autumn 1917, Sarah Schenirer opens a supplementary Jewish class in her two-room apartment for twenty-five girls, soon forty, most drawn from families she knows through her dressmaking work. The school offers religious study alongside pupils’ government schooling. See the University of Toronto timeline, YIVO Encyclopedia and the Jewish Religious Community of Kraków.

Kraków’s Agudath Israel leadership assumes financial responsibility for Schenirer’s school and names it Bais Yaakov, after the traditional interpretation of ‘House of Jacob’ in Exodus 19:3 as referring to women. Institutional backing allows the local experiment to become a network. See the Bais Yaakov Project timeline and YIVO Encyclopedia.

Agudath Israel commits to sponsoring a national Bais Yaakov network. Schenirer travels and lectures to win local support, while German neo-Orthodox educator Leo Deutschlander and Keren HaTorah help professionalize curricula and fundraising. This cooperation—rather than one founder acting alone—drives expansion. See the YIVO Encyclopedia, Oxford Bibliographies in Jewish Studies and the Bais Yaakov Project.

Schenirer opens a teachers’ seminary in her apartment to supply the expanding school system with trained women educators. The First World Congress of Agudath Israel also establishes Keren HaTorah to supervise and fund Orthodox education. See the University of Toronto timeline, YIVO Encyclopedia and Oxford Bibliographies.

The seminary outgrows Schenirer’s apartment and moves to a larger eight-room property at 30 Augustiańska Street. Schenirer lives alongside students, combining teaching, mentorship and administration; by 1924 the wider movement already reported fifty-four schools. See the Bais Yaakov Project timeline and the Jewish Religious Community of Kraków.

Schenirer helps shape Bnos Agudath Israel, the affiliated youth movement for Bais Yaakov graduates. The movement creates continuing religious, social and leadership frameworks beyond school and helps connect local groups across Poland. See the YIVO Encyclopedia and the University of Toronto timeline.

A public cornerstone ceremony begins construction of a purpose-built Bais Yaakov seminary at 10 Świętego Stanisława Street. Fundraising links Kraków’s project to Orthodox supporters in Western Europe and the United States. See the Bais Yaakov Project timeline and the Jewish Religious Community of Kraków.

The five-storey central seminary building opens, institutionalizing the training system Schenirer began in her apartment. That year she marries Yitzhak Landau. The network includes supplementary and full-time schools, seminaries, vocational programmes and youth organizations rather than a single uniform school model. See the University of Toronto timeline, Oxford Bibliographies and Jewish Women’s Archive biography.

Schenirer steps down from formal leadership as Yehudah Leib Orlean assumes direction of the Kraków seminary and central office, though she remains the movement’s symbolic and active mentor. Her Gezamlte shriftn collects educational articles, memoirs, stories and plays in Yiddish. See the YIVO Encyclopedia and the Bais Yaakov Project timeline.

Sarah Schenirer dies of tuberculosis in Kraków on 1 March 1935, aged fifty-one. She is buried in the new Jewish cemetery at Płaszów. The Nazis later destroy the cemetery and her grave; a symbolic memorial stone is installed near the recovered location in the twenty-first century. See the Jewish Religious Community of Kraków, YIVO Encyclopedia and the Jewish Women’s Archive biography.

David Ben-Gurion.place: Płońsk, Congress Poland, Russian Empire; now Poland
David Ben-Gurion.event: David Ben-Gurion is born David Grün on 16 October 1886 in Płońsk to Avigdor Grün, a lawyer and Hovevei Zion activist, and Scheindel Fridman. He grows up in a family committed to Hebrew education and Zionism. See the Knesset Lexicon, Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute and ANU Museum of the Jewish People.

At eighteen, David Grün moves to Warsaw, supports himself by teaching at a Jewish school and becomes active in Poalei Zion. Plans for advanced study give way to his decision to immigrate to Palestine. See the Knesset commemorative biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute chronology.

David Ben-Gurion.place: Jaffa and Petah Tikva, Ottoman Palestine
David Ben-Gurion.event: Grün lands at Jaffa in September 1906 during the Second Aliyah and proceeds to Petah Tikva, where he works intermittently as an agricultural labourer and becomes active in the Palestinian branch of Poalei Zion. See the Knesset biography, Jewish Virtual Library and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

David Ben-Gurion.place: Sejera, Ottoman Palestine; now Ilaniya, Israel
David Ben-Gurion.event: Ben-Gurion works in the agricultural colony of Sejera, one of several settlements in which he labours. There he participates in efforts to organize Jewish guarding and develops the labour-and-defence ideas central to his political outlook. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

He joins the editorial staff of Ha’ahdut, Poalei Zion’s Hebrew newspaper, and begins signing articles ‘David Ben-Gurion,’ adopting the name of an ancient Jewish figure associated with the revolt against Rome. See the Knesset commemorative biography and National Library of Israel.

David Ben-Gurion.place: Salonika, Ottoman Empire; now Thessaloniki, Greece
David Ben-Gurion.event: Ben-Gurion moves to Salonika to learn Turkish in preparation for legal studies. The city’s large Jewish population and organized port labour make a strong impression on his ideas about a productive Hebrew-speaking society. See the Knesset Lexicon and the Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute chronology.

David Ben-Gurion.place: Constantinople, Ottoman Empire; now Istanbul, Turkey
David Ben-Gurion.event: Ben-Gurion and Yitzhak Ben-Zvi study law at Istanbul University, hoping that legal and Ottoman political training will assist Zionist work within the empire. The Balkan Wars and then the First World War interrupt the course. See the Knesset Lexicon and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

Ottoman authorities expel Ben-Gurion and Yitzhak Ben-Zvi from Palestine for their Zionist political activity. They pass through Alexandria before travelling to the United States, turning wartime exile into an organizing campaign abroad. See the Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute and Jewish Virtual Library.

In New York, Ben-Gurion and Ben-Zvi organize the Hehalutz movement and campaign among American Jews for Labor Zionism. Ben-Gurion meets nurse and activist Paula Munweis, whom he marries in 1917, and coauthors a study of Palestine. See the Knesset biography and Jewish Virtual Library.

After the Balfour Declaration and American entry into the war, Ben-Gurion volunteers for the British Army’s Jewish Legion and trains at Fort Edward in Windsor before deployment toward Palestine. See Jewish Virtual Library and the Knesset biography.

Back in Palestine, Ben-Gurion helps establish Ahdut HaAvoda and becomes one of its leading figures, working to unite labour institutions into a national political force. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

The founding conference of the Histadrut convenes in Haifa. Ben-Gurion becomes its first secretary-general and, from 1921 to 1935, develops the labour federation into an economic, settlement, welfare and defence framework of the Yishuv. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

After helping unite labour parties in Mapai, Ben-Gurion becomes chairman of the Jewish Agency Executive in Jerusalem. He emerges as the Yishuv’s dominant political leader and later accepts partition in principle as a route to Jewish sovereignty. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

Ben-Gurion participates in the St James’s Conference and rejects Britain’s subsequent White Paper, which sharply limits Jewish immigration and land purchase. During the Second World War he supports fighting Nazi Germany while opposing British restrictions on the Yishuv. See the Knesset biography and National Library of Israel.

Ben-Gurion helps lead the Biltmore Conference, whose programme calls for Palestine to be established as a Jewish Commonwealth and shifts organized Zionism toward an explicit demand for statehood. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

Ben-Gurion assumes the defence portfolio within the Jewish Agency and concentrates on expanding, training and arming the Haganah in expectation of conflict surrounding the end of British rule. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

On 14 May 1948, as chairman of the People’s Administration, David Ben-Gurion reads the Declaration of Independence at the Tel Aviv Museum and becomes prime minister and defence minister of the provisional government. During the ensuing war he establishes the Israel Defense Forces and enforces unified state command, including through the Altalena confrontation and dissolution of separate military headquarters. The war also produces the mass displacement of Palestinian Arabs; the extent and character of Ben-Gurion’s responsibility for expulsions and prevention of return remain subjects of major historical debate. See the Israel State Archives, Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

Ben-Gurion forms Israel’s first elected government and promotes the transfer of the Knesset and government ministries to Jerusalem. His early governments absorb mass immigration, impose austerity, build state institutions and maintain military government over most Palestinian Arab citizens. See the Knesset biography and the Prime Minister’s Office government history.

Ben-Gurion’s government secures the reparations agreement with West Germany despite intense public opposition led by Menachem Begin. Ben-Gurion argues that compensation is essential for absorbing survivors and strengthening the state; opponents condemn negotiation with Germany so soon after the Holocaust. See the Knesset commemorative biography and selected speech and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

Ben-Gurion resigns from government and joins Kibbutz Sde Boker, presenting settlement of the Negev as a personal and national pioneering mission. He retains political influence and returns to government in 1955. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

After Pinhas Lavon resigns as defence minister amid the failed Israeli covert operation in Egypt, Ben-Gurion returns first as defence minister and then again as prime minister. The unresolved Lavon Affair later fractures his party and contributes to his final resignation. See the Israel Ministry of Defense Archives and Knesset biography.

As prime minister and defence minister, Ben-Gurion authorizes Israel’s Sinai campaign in secret coordination with France and Britain. Israeli forces occupy Sinai but withdraw under international pressure; the campaign temporarily improves freedom of navigation and border security while entangling Israel in the Anglo-French Suez intervention. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

Ben-Gurion resigns as prime minister in June 1963 amid disputes over security policy, relations with West Germany and the continuing Lavon Affair. Levi Eshkol succeeds him, but their conflict soon divides Mapai. See the Knesset biography, Ministry of Defense Archives and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

Ben-Gurion leaves Mapai with allies including Shimon Peres and Moshe Dayan and founds Rafi, which wins ten seats in the 1965 election. He later rejects Rafi’s merger into the Israeli Labor Party and leads the small National List. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

At age eighty-three, Ben-Gurion retires from the Knesset and active party politics. At Sde Boker he concentrates on memoirs, historical writing and the educational institutions intended to advance study and development of the Negev. See the Knesset biography and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute and Archives.

After suffering a cerebral hemorrhage, David Ben-Gurion dies at Sheba Medical Center on 1 December 1973, shortly after the Yom Kippur War. See the Knesset Lexicon, National Library of Israel and Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute.

David Ben-Gurion.place: Midreshet Ben-Gurion near Sde Boker, Israel
David Ben-Gurion.event: Ben-Gurion is buried beside Paula on the desert plateau overlooking Nahal Zin, at the site they selected near Sde Boker. His home, archive and associated institute become central sites for preserving and researching his documentary legacy. See the Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute, Ben-Gurion Archives and the David Ben-Gurion Law.

Viktor Frankl.event: Viktor Emil Frankl is born in Vienna on 26 March 1905, the middle child of Jewish civil servant Gabriel Frankl and Elsa Frankl, née Lion. See the Viktor Frankl Institute biography and University of Vienna.

At fifteen, Frankl delivers his first public lecture, ‘On the Meaning of Life,’ while participating in the Young Socialist Workers. His interest in meaning and social responsibility therefore precedes both his medical career and the Holocaust. See the Viktor Frankl Institute chronology.

Frankl studies medicine at the University of Vienna, serves as spokesman for the Austrian Socialist High School Students Association and attends Alfred Adler’s circle. His early contact with Sigmund Freud and Adler informs, but does not determine, his emerging approach. See the Viktor Frankl Institute and University of Vienna.

At congress lectures in Düsseldorf, Frankfurt and Berlin, Frankl presents a meaning-centred approach to psychotherapy and uses the term ‘logotherapy.’ This documented prewar use corrects the common misconception that he invented the method in a concentration camp. See the Viktor Frankl Institute biography.

Frankl organizes free youth-counselling centres in Vienna, recruiting psychologists including Charlotte Bühler and Erwin Wexberg. The programme particularly addresses adolescent crisis and suicide risk and is later extended to other cities. See the Viktor Frankl Institute chronology.

Frankl receives his medical doctorate and begins specialist work in neurology and psychiatry. His clinical training and prewar suicide-prevention work form the medical basis of logotherapy. See the Viktor Frankl Institute life-and-work profile and University of Vienna.

Viktor Frankl.place: Rothschild Hospital, Vienna, Austria under Nazi rule
Viktor Frankl.event: Frankl becomes director of neurology at the Rothschild Hospital, then Vienna’s principal hospital for Jewish patients. According to the Frankl Institute, he risks his life by altering diagnoses to prevent mentally ill patients from being killed through Nazi ‘euthanasia’ procedures. See the Viktor Frankl Institute biography.

Frankl writes the first manuscript of Ärztliche Seelsorge, setting out logotherapy and existential analysis, and marries Rothschild Hospital nurse Tilly Grosser. The couple are forced by Nazi policy to abort their child. See the Viktor Frankl Institute chronology.

Viktor Frankl.place: Theresienstadt Ghetto, Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia; now Terezín, Czechia
Viktor Frankl.event: In September, Frankl, Tilly and his parents are deported from Vienna to Theresienstadt. He organizes psychological first aid for new arrivals and suicide prevention with other prisoners, including ר׳ רגינה יונאס; his father dies there from exhaustion. See the Viktor Frankl Institute and the Holocaust Encyclopedia testimony record.

In October, Frankl and Tilly are deported from Theresienstadt through Auschwitz-Birkenau; his mother follows and is murdered. Frankl’s hidden manuscript is confiscated, and after only a few days in transit he is selected for forced-labour transfer. The brief stay should not be confused with long-term imprisonment at Auschwitz. See the Viktor Frankl Institute and Holocaust Encyclopedia.

On 25 October, after the Auschwitz transit, Frankl reaches Kaufering III, a Dachau subcamp where prisoners perform deadly forced labour connected with underground armaments construction. This camp—not Auschwitz—accounts for most of this phase of his imprisonment. See the Holocaust Encyclopedia and the Viktor Frankl Institute.

Transferred to Türkheim, another Dachau subcamp, Frankl contracts typhus and keeps himself mentally alert by reconstructing notes for Ärztliche Seelsorge. U.S. forces liberate the camp on 27 April; he briefly serves as a doctor in a displaced-persons hospital. See the Viktor Frankl Institute chronology and the Holocaust Encyclopedia.

Frankl returns to Vienna and learns that Tilly died after transfer to Bergen-Belsen and that his mother, brother and sister-in-law were murdered. Supported by friends, he reconstructs his lost manuscript rather than treating the camps as the origin of logotherapy. See the Viktor Frankl Institute biography.

Frankl becomes director of the Vienna Neurological Policlinic, a post he holds until 1970. He publishes the reconstructed Ärztliche Seelsorge and dictates Ein Psycholog erlebt das Konzentrationslager in nine days; the latter is eventually known in English as Man’s Search for Meaning. See the Viktor Frankl Institute biography and official books page.

Frankl marries Eleonore Katharina Schwindt, known as Elly; their daughter Gabriele is born in December. Elly becomes his lifelong collaborator in the international development of logotherapy. See the Viktor Frankl Institute chronology.

Frankl earns a doctorate in philosophy with a dissertation published as Der unbewusste Gott and is promoted to associate professor of neurology and psychiatry. His logotherapy and existential analysis are described as the ‘Third Viennese School of Psychotherapy.’ See the Viktor Frankl Institute and University of Vienna.

Beacon Press publishes the first U.S. edition of Frankl’s camp book under the title From Death-Camp to Existentialism; later editions use Man’s Search for Meaning. The translation transforms a modest German publication into his best-known international work. See the Viktor Frankl Institute chronology and official publication history.

Viktor Frankl.place: Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States
Viktor Frankl.event: Frankl serves as a guest professor at Harvard University, one of many overseas appointments through which he introduces logotherapy to English-speaking academic and clinical audiences. See the Viktor Frankl Institute biography.

Viktor Frankl.place: San Quentin State Prison, California, United States
Viktor Frankl.event: Frankl addresses prisoners at San Quentin on responsibility, guilt and the possibility of moral change. That year he also writes The Will to Meaning, his most systematic book originally composed in English. See the Viktor Frankl Institute chronology.

United States International University establishes a chair in logotherapy for Frankl, recognizing the field’s growing international institutional presence. San Diego also hosts the First World Congress on Logotherapy in 1980. See the Viktor Frankl Institute biography.

At the fiftieth-anniversary commemoration of the Anschluss, Frankl rejects indiscriminate ‘collective guilt,’ distinguishing personal responsibility from inherited blame while insisting that Austrians confront individual complicity. See the Viktor Frankl Institute chronology.

Frankl celebrates a second bar mitzvah in Jerusalem at age eighty-three, a significant public expression of the Jewish identity that remained present alongside the universal language of his psychotherapy. See the Viktor Frankl Institute biography and the National Library of Israel authority record.

Viktor Frankl dies of heart failure in Vienna on 2 September 1997, aged ninety-two, shortly after publication of Man’s Search for Ultimate Meaning. His books, clinical school and archival institute carry his work into many languages and countries. See the Viktor Frankl Institute and University of Vienna.

Anne Frank.place: Maingau Red Cross Hospital, Frankfurt am Main, Germany
Anne Frank.event: Annelies Marie Frank is born on 12 June 1929 to Otto Heinrich Frank and Edith Frank-Holländer. Her sister Margot, born in 1926, is three years older. See the Anne Frank House timeline and United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.

Anne spends her earliest years in the Frank family home at 307 Marbachweg in a mixed middle-class neighbourhood where Jewish and non-Jewish children play together. The family remains there until March 1931. See the Anne Frank House detailed timeline.

The Frank family moves to a smaller apartment at 24 Ganghoferstraße as the economic crisis damages Otto Frank’s business prospects and political extremism intensifies. See the Anne Frank House timeline.

After the Nazis take power, Edith takes Anne and Margot to her mother Rosa Holländer in Aachen while Otto establishes Opekta in Amsterdam. Their departure is part of a Jewish refugee movement caused by escalating Nazi persecution, not an ordinary family relocation. See the Anne Frank House and USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia.

Anne arrives in Amsterdam on 16 February, the last immediate family member to join the new home. She learns Dutch quickly, begins kindergarten at the Sixth Montessori School in April and builds a wide circle of friends. See the Anne Frank House timeline and Anne Frank House biography.

Germany invades the Netherlands in May. Successive occupation decrees register, segregate and dispossess Jews; Anne’s refugee safety disappears as persecution follows the family into Amsterdam. See the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia and the Anne Frank House historical timeline.

Nazi regulations force Anne and Margot out of their previous schools and into the Jewish Lyceum. The measure isolates Jewish pupils from their non-Jewish classmates as deportation policy develops. See the Anne Frank House educational chronology.

On her thirteenth birthday, 12 June, Anne receives the red-and-white checked notebook chosen in a local bookshop. She begins writing in Dutch, addressing entries to an imagined friend and recording ordinary adolescence amid intensifying persecution. See the Anne Frank House diary account and Anne Frank House Knowledge Base.

Anne Frank.place: Secret Annex, 263 Prinsengracht, Amsterdam, German-occupied Netherlands
Anne Frank.event: On 6 July, one day after Margot receives a summons for supposed labour in Germany, the Frank family enters a prepared hiding place behind Otto’s business. The Van Pels family joins on 13 July and Fritz Pfeffer on 16 November. Six helpers sustain the eight people at extreme personal risk. See the Anne Frank House account of residents and helpers and USHMM.

Anne Frank.place: Secret Annex, 263 Prinsengracht, Amsterdam, German-occupied Netherlands
Anne Frank.event: After hearing Dutch minister Gerrit Bolkestein’s radio appeal to preserve occupation diaries, Anne begins revising her text for publication on 20 May. She titles the planned book Het Achterhuis and rewrites roughly 50,000 words, demonstrating deliberate literary craft rather than accidental private fame. See the Anne Frank House guide to the complete works.

Anne Frank.place: Secret Annex, 263 Prinsengracht, Amsterdam, German-occupied Netherlands
Anne Frank.event: Anne writes her last surviving diary entry on 1 August. On 4 August, German Security Service personnel and Dutch policemen raid the building and arrest the eight people in hiding and two helpers. No surviving evidence proves who, if anyone, betrayed them; accidental discovery remains possible. See the Anne Frank House research assessment and USHMM.

On 8 August, the prisoners are sent to Westerbork. Because they were captured in hiding, the eight are placed in the punishment barracks and assigned forced labour rather than treated as ordinary internees. See the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia and the Anne Frank House timeline.

Anne, her family and the other Annex residents leave Westerbork on 3 September aboard its last transport to Auschwitz, carrying 1,019 Jews, and arrive on 5 September. Anne, Margot and Edith are selected for forced labour; the family is permanently separated from Otto. See the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia.

Anne and Margot are selected with other women for transfer from Auschwitz on the night of 1–2 November and reach Bergen-Belsen several days later; Edith remains behind and dies at Auschwitz. Overcrowding, starvation, exposure and infectious disease dominate the sisters’ final months. See the Anne Frank House timeline and USHMM.

Anne and Margot contract typhus and die, probably in February 1945, only weeks before British liberation on 15 April. Their exact death dates and burial places are unknown; research supersedes the formerly conventional March date without supplying a false precision. See the Anne Frank House biography, its research timeline, and USHMM.

Chaim Weizmann.event: Born in Motal, Russian Empire (today Belarus)
Moved to Zurich, Switzerland for doctoral studies
Received PhD in chemistry from University of Fribourg, Switzerland
Moved to Manchester, England as lecturer in chemistry
Became prominent leader in the British Zionist Federation
Played key role in securing the Balfour Declaration from the British government
Elected President of the World Zionist Organization at the Carlsbad Congress
Resigned as WZO President after internal disputes
Re-elected President of the World Zionist Organization
Led Zionist opposition to the British White Paper restricting immigration to Palestine
Chaired the Biltmore Conference in New York, calling for a Jewish Commonwealth
Lobbied at the UN for partition of Palestine
Elected as the first President of the State of Israel
Died in Rehovot, Israel; buried at Weizmann Institute of Science

Sir Moses Haim Montefiore.event: Born in Livorno, Tuscany, Italy, to a Sephardic Jewish family.
Became broker at London Stock Exchange.
Married Judith Cohen; linked to Rothschild family.
First visit to Jerusalem; became strictly observant Jew.
Purchased East Cliff Lodge, Ramsgate; later built Montefiore Synagogue (1833).
Elected President of the Board of Deputies of British Jews.
Elected Sheriff of the City of London; knighted by Queen Victoria.
Mission to Damascus to intervene in the Damascus Affair blood libel case.
Met Tsar Nicholas I in Russia to intercede for Jews; awarded baronetcy the same year.
Established agricultural training project near Jaffa using Judah Touro’s bequest.
Advocated in Rome for release of Jewish boy Edgardo Mortara.
Founded Mishkenot Sha’ananim, first Jewish neighborhood outside Jerusalem’s walls.
Mission to Safi, Morocco, against blood libel accusations.
Second mission to Russia; met Tsar Alexander II.
Celebrated 100th birthday with major public celebrations in Ramsgate.
Died in Ramsgate at age 100; buried beside wife Judith in Montefiore Mausoleum.

Solomon Schechter.event: Studied at yeshiva in Piatra Neamț
Studied under Rabbi Joseph Saul Nathanson in Lemberg
Studied at Rabbinical College in Vienna under Meir Friedmann
Studied at Berlin Hochschule and University of Berlin
Invited to Britain to tutor rabbinics under Claude Montefiore in London
Appointed lecturer in Talmudics and reader in Rabbinics at Cambridge University
Excavated the Cairo Geniza with support from Hermann Adler and Aaron Raphael Ben Shim'on
Professor of Hebrew at University College London
Became President of the Jewish Theological Seminary of America in New York
Died and buried at Mount Hebron Cemetery, Queens, New York

Theodor Herzl.event: Studied law at the University of Vienna
Worked as Paris correspondent for the Neue Freie Presse
Organized the First Zionist Congress in Basel, Switzerland
Died in Edlach, near Reichenau an der Rax, Austria; initially buried in Vienna, later reinterred in Jerusalem
